extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics; readers studying Kant's Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for aesthetic judgements (pleasant, beautiful, sublime, absolutely good), including conditions for purity, universality/communicability, the role of moral Ideas, and anti-patterns (teleological or sensuous determinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of aesthetic judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: In reference to the feeling of pleasure an object is to be classified as either pleasant, or beautiful, or sublime, or good (absolutely) (jucundum, pulchrum, sublime, honestum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant sets these four exhaustive categories for feelings of pleasure: 'pleasant' (motive of desire), 'beautiful' (pleasure in the mere judgement), 'sublime' (pleasure through opposition to sensible interest), and the 'absolutely good' (moral, with a priori necessity). Each has distinct formal conditions and implications for communicability and relation to concepts, sensibility, and Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasant, as motive of desire, is always of one and the same kind, no matter whence it comes and however specifically different the representation may be; account is taken only of the number of its charms, and so only of the mass of the pleasant sensation; it can be made intelligible only by quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure as 'pleasant' is empirical and quantitative, not related to culture or to pure aesthetic judgement. It belongs to mere enjoyment and does not ground claims to universal communicability or a priori principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful is what pleases in the mere judgement (and therefore not by the medium of sensation in accordance with a concept of the Understanding). It requires the representation of a certain quality of the Object that can be made intelligible and reduced to concepts (although it is not so reduced in an aesthetical judgement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: disinterestedness (pleases apart from all interest), formal purposiveness (pleasure arises from perceived purposiveness of form without concept), positive satisfaction, cultivative effect (teaches attention to purposiveness), and suitability for a Deduction (the Beautiful in nature has purposiveness grounded in object form and thus admits a justificatory Deduction). Anti-pattern: if judgement is determined by sensation or by teleological concepts, it ceases to be a pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is what pleases immediately through its opposition to the interest of sense. It consists merely in the relation by which the sensible in the representation of nature is judged available for a possible supersensible use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sublime is experienced when the Imagination is strained by the representation (mathematically by extension or dynamically by might) toward Ideas of Reason that cannot be adequately presented. Satisfaction is negative (a feeling of deprivation of imaginative freedom paired with the mind's superiority via Reason). Examples: mountain peaks, deep chasms, the starry heaven, the ocean — but only when regarded as mere appearances (not teleologically). The judgement of the sublime presupposes moral Ideas and a cultivated susceptibility; uneducated observers may only feel terror. The Sublime's exposition doubled as its Deduction; pure aesthetic sublimity must avoid teleological or conceptual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility for Ideas / moral feeling required for the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: That the mind be attuned to feel the sublime postulates a susceptibility of the mind for Ideas. Without development of moral Ideas, that which we, prepared by culture, call sublime, presents itself to the uneducated man merely as terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant insists that experiencing the sublime presupposes moral cultivation: the Imagination is related to Reason (Ideas) and the moral feeling underlies the judgement. Thus part of the criterion for calling something sublime is that the subject can (or is presumed to) relate the representation to supersensible Ideas (moral destination), not merely experience bodily fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of aesthetic judgement (disinterestedness and freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic purposiveness is the conformity to law of the Judgement in its freedom. If the judgement be determined by anything else—whether sensation or concept—although it may be conformable to law, it cannot be the act of a free Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure aesthetic judgement must be disinterested (not based on desire or sensation) and not determined by concepts (including teleological concepts). The Imagination should be free, engaged in 'play' for beauty, or strained toward Reason for the sublime, but not subordinated to empirical interest or conceptual ends. Anti-patterns include judgments based on sensory gratification, desire, or teleological/cognitive attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to universal communicability and need for an a priori principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim of an aesthetical judgement to universal validity for every subject requires, as a judgement resting on some a priori principle, a Deduction (or legitimatising of its pretensions) in addition to its Exposition; if it is concerned with satisfaction or dissatisfaction in the form of the Object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgements of taste purport a subjective universality (they demand the agreement of every one) despite being non-cognitive. Kant argues this requires grounding in an a priori principle (not empirical consensus). For the Beautiful in nature this motivates searching for a Deduction; empirical psychology alone cannot justify this universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction applies to the Beautiful (not the Sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deduction of aesthetical judgements on the objects of nature must not be directed to what we call Sublime in nature, but only to the Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant reasons that the Beautiful has purposiveness grounded in the object's form (making a Deduction possible), whereas the Sublime in nature is merely an occasion making us conscious of a mental state (Ideas/moral purposiveness) and thus its Exposition already functions as its Deduction. Practically: when justifying a universal claim of taste one focuses on beauty in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive (beautiful) vs negative (sublime) satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the Beautiful is positive; the satisfaction in the Sublime is negative (a feeling that the Imagination is depriving itself of its freedom, while it is purposively determined according to a different law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beautiful: enjoyment, free play of faculties, positive content. Sublime: involves an awareness of limitation (imagination fails), but this failure points to Reason/Ideas and gives a negative-yet-elevating pleasure (awe, astonishment bordering on terror). Use this distinction when characterising responses and effects on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleological/conceptual determinations (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we call the sight of the starry heaven sublime, we must not place at the basis of our judgement concepts of worlds inhabited by rational beings ... For example, to call the ocean sublime we must regard it, just as we see it, as a distant, all-embracing vault (or as an abyss threatening to overwhelm everything), and not think of it as a kingdom of aquatic creatures or as source of vapours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing beauty or sublimity in nature for a pure aesthetic judgement, do not introduce teleological explanations, cognitive knowledge, or conceptual purposes. Such determinations convert the judgement into a teleological or empirical one and destroy the purity required for aesthetic universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (purposiveness without art) as a stylistic criterion for the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity (purposiveness without art) is as it were the style of Nature in the sublime, and so also of Morality which is a second (supersensible) nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime presentations and moral grandeur are best expressed by simplicity—an artless purposiveness. This is a normative stylistic criterion: grandeur or nobility should avoid unnecessary ornament that would detract from moral/supersensible elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional taxonomy and aesthetic value (strenuous vs languid affections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every affection of the strenuous kind (viz. that excites the consciousness of our power to overcome every obstacle—animi strenui) is aesthetically sublime, e.g. wrath, even despair (the despair of indignation). But affections of the languid kind (which make the very effort of resistance an object of pain—animum languidum) have nothing noble in themselves, but they may be reckoned under the sensuously beautiful. Tender emotions that rise to affections are worthless (sentimentality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating emotional content as sublime or beautiful: prefer strong, energetic, overcoming affections for the sublime; languid, enervating emotions point to sensuous beauty or sentimental weakness. Anti-examples include romances, lacrymose plays, and shallow moral precepts that encourage sentimental languor rather than noble moral strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthusiasm (aesthetic sublime) vs fanaticism (anti-sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idea of the Good conjoined with affection is called enthusiasm. Aesthetically, enthusiasm is sublime because it is a tension of forces produced by Ideas. Fanaticism, a delusion comparable to monomania, is least compatible with the sublime because in its detail it is ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish transitory, Idea-driven enthusiasm—which can be an aesthetically sublime state—from fanatic, brooding fixation (fanaticism) which is destructive of sound judgement and therefore not sublime. Enthusiasm is a temporary elevation linked to Ideas; fanaticism is an entrenched mental disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation from society as sublime only when grounded in Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation from all society is regarded as sublime, if it rests upon Ideas that overlook all sensible interest. To be sufficient for oneself, and consequently to have no need of society, without at the same time being unsociable, i.e. without flying from it, is something bordering on the sublime; as is any dispensing with wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solitude or renunciation can count as sublime if motivated by moral/supersensible Ideas (a dignified self-sufficiency). If isolation stems from misanthropy, fear, or mere shyness, it is contemptible or hateful and not sublime. Use the subject's disposition and maxims as the criterion for whether solitude is aesthetically sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic purposiveness: conformity to law without concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical purposiveness is the conformity to law of the Judgement in its freedom. The satisfaction in the object depends on the relation in which we wish to place the Imagination; always provided that it by itself entertains the mind in free occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic purposiveness describes how judgement finds purposiveness in form without recourse to determinate concepts. When evaluating or producing aesthetic objects, ensure the form permits free imaginative play (beauty) or imaginative strain pointing to Reason (sublime) rather than serving external conceptual ends.
